newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya says takes steps to raise coffee production.
newsitem.headline: Kenya says takes steps to raise coffee production.

text.p: Kenyan authorities said on Tuesday they were taking steps to increase coffee production, which has been undermined by poor weather in the past year.

"The government is taking measures to increase coffee production in the near future," said Vice-President George Saitoti in a presentation to a five-day international conference on coffee science in Nairobi.
Output in 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) is estimated at 75,000 to 78,000 tonnes on account of drought that hit most of East Africa from October last year to March 1997, when the seasonal long rains arrived.
Kenya produced 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 in 1994/95, according to official statistics.
On Tuesday, Kenyan export auctions resumed after a two-week break forced by an acute shortage of coffee in the market.
Some 20,035 60-kg bags were sold, down from 22,205 at the last auction on July 1.
One trader said the coffee on offer was drought-affected and the beans were "light and ragged".
The seasonal long rains have been inadequate and have become the greatest worry to growers, according to field officers with the Coffee Board of Kenya.

Saitoti said current efforts included the intensification of coffee production per unit area, expansion of output in areas west of the Rift Valley and the introduction of new, high-yielding and disease-resistant crop varieties.
He added that Kenya was increasing yields of small holders, and that further liberalisation and privatisation in the sector had improved payments to farmers.
Kenya's share of world coffee trade if about 2.3 percent but its mild arabicas earn premiums well above world market rates.
Arabicas cover 176,500 hectares in Kenya while robustas account for just 1,000 hectares. Some 70 percent of the total area under coffee is cultivated by 335,000 small holders.
The average yield per hectare is 0.41 tonnes for small holders and 0.9 for large estate growers, according to an agriculture ministry policy document at the conference.
"In the long run, increased production will depend on improving productivity rather than expanding the hectarage under cultivation," the agriculture ministry document said.

Kenya's coffee is processed by 1,968 factories, of which 835 are run by small holder cooperative societies and 1,133 by estates. Coffee parchment is milled by five commercial millers with a total capacity of 240,000 tonnes.
The Coffee Board of Kenya classifies, bulks and warehouses the coffee and offers it for sale at the central export auction.
